title: System Tables for Cost, Audit and Workload Monitoring

concepts.heading: Billing Usage and Correction Records
concepts.body: `system.billing.usage` holds one row per billable usage period, with the SKU, the quantity, `usage_metadata` (which job, cluster, warehouse or pipeline caused it) and `custom_tags`. The billing tables are global: a workspace in any region shows the whole account. Databricks also corrects past records. When a record was wrong, it adds two new rows instead of editing the old one: a `RETRACTION` with an identical row but a negative `usage_quantity` that cancels the original, and a `RESTATEMENT` with the corrected values. Only the `ORIGINAL` rows are the normal case, so a filter such as `record_type = 'ORIGINAL'` looks tidy but keeps the wrong numbers for any corrected month. Sum every row instead: the retraction cancels the original and the restatement supplies the right amount. A correction can also consist of a retraction alone when the usage should never have been recorded. To turn quantity into money, join `system.billing.list_prices` on the SKU and the price validity window; the price table is a history, so one SKU has several rows over time.

concepts.heading: Attributing Cost to Jobs, Clusters and Pipelines
concepts.body: Attribution depends on what the compute was. `usage_metadata.job_id` is filled for serverless jobs and for jobs on job compute, but not for a job that runs on all-purpose compute. That usage is billed under the ALL_PURPOSE product and carries only `cluster_id`, so a dashboard that groups by `job_id` shows the cost vanishing when a job is moved to a shared cluster. For such cases attribute through `cluster_id` and join the cluster's tags or owner from `system.compute.clusters`. Pipelines carry their own identifier in `usage_metadata`, and `billing_origin_product` separates products such as jobs, pipelines and SQL. The most reliable lever for chargeback is tagging: `custom_tags` set on compute appear on the usage rows, so cost can be grouped by team without joins. Moving recurring jobs from all-purpose clusters to job compute is both cheaper and gives job-level billing records, which is why platform teams look for jobs whose tasks still run on interactive clusters.

concepts.heading: Lakeflow Tables: SCD2, Regional Scope and Run History
concepts.body: The `system.lakeflow` schema describes jobs and pipelines. `jobs`, `job_tasks` and `pipelines` are slowly changing dimension tables: every rename or schedule edit adds a row, and a delete adds a row with `delete_time` set. Joining usage to them directly multiplies the cost for every edited job. Reduce the table to its latest row per entity first (a window over `change_time` descending, `ROW_NUMBER() = 1`), then drop deleted entities, and only then join. The run tables `job_run_timeline`, `job_task_run_timeline` and `pipeline_update_timeline` are immutable and need no deduplication; the task timeline reports durations per task run and lists the compute in `compute_ids`. Unlike billing, these tables are regional: they contain the workspaces of the same cloud region only, so a name lookup for an eu job must run from an eu workspace even though its usage is visible everywhere. Free retention is 365 days, except that the newest row of every SCD2 entity is always kept.

concepts.heading: Compute, Lineage and Access to System Tables
concepts.body: `system.compute.node_timeline` stores utilization per node per minute with a flag for the driver, so a team can see that a driver (for example after large collects) was saturated while workers idled, even after the cluster has terminated. `system.compute.clusters` keeps configuration history, including `cluster_source`. The lineage tables `table_lineage` and `column_lineage` are a subset of all reads and writes: records appear only when lineage can be inferred, so an empty result is weak evidence that a table is unused and a staged deprecation is the safe route. Access is governed by Unity Catalog. By default only users who are both account admin and metastore admin can read system tables, and the tables are read-only. To share them, grant `USE CATALOG` on `system`, `USE SCHEMA` and `SELECT` on the schemas. To give a team lead only the lead's own workspaces, grant `SELECT` on a view in a governed schema that filters the usage rows. The audit log table is still in Public Preview, so exam answers rest on the other tables.

examPoints: Corrections arrive as RETRACTION plus RESTATEMENT rows: sum all record types, never filter to ORIGINAL.
job_id is empty for jobs on all-purpose compute; attribute through cluster_id and cluster tags. jobs, job_tasks and pipelines are SCD2: take the latest row first.
Billing is global but lakeflow tables are regional; share system tables through a filtered view, not broad grants.

quiz.q: A finance report totals usage_quantity from system.billing.usage with WHERE record_type = 'ORIGINAL' to avoid negative values. For a month with corrections the total no longer matches the invoice. What should the engineer change?
choices: Keep the filter and add RESTATEMENT rows only, because a retraction cancels the corrected amount a second time
Remove the filter and sum every row, so each retraction cancels its original and the restatement adds the corrected amount
Join system.billing.list_prices first and drop every row whose price is missing, because corrections never carry a SKU price
Filter on usage_end_time of the previous month only, because corrected usage is always written into the month that follows
quiz.explain: The original, the retraction (negative quantity, otherwise identical) and the restatement together net to the corrected amount. Filtering to ORIGINAL keeps the wrong figure; keeping only restatements ignores uncorrected usage. Price joins and end-time windows do not govern corrections.

quiz.q: A report joins system.billing.usage to system.lakeflow.jobs on workspace and job ID and shows totals above the billed amount for jobs that were renamed or rescheduled. What is the fix?
choices: Add DISTINCT to the select list, because the jobs table repeats the same job once for every workspace in the whole region
Read the report from a workspace in another region, because the jobs table duplicates its rows across regions to survive regional outages
Reduce jobs to the latest row per workspace and job by change_time, exclude deleted jobs, and then join usage to that result
Replace the join with job_run_timeline, because the jobs table is only filled for jobs that never changed their definition
quiz.explain: jobs is an SCD2 table: each edit adds a row, so a plain join multiplies usage by the number of versions. Taking the newest row per entity first fixes it. DISTINCT does not undo multiplied sums, and regions do not duplicate rows.

recap: Billing is global, additive and corrected through retraction and restatement rows; lakeflow history is regional and SCD2, so reduce to the latest row before joining. Know which compute fills job_id, and expose system tables through views.

title: Monitoring with REST, CLI, SDK and Pipeline Event Logs

concepts.heading: Reading Runs Through the Jobs API
concepts.body: `runs/list` answers questions such as how many runs failed last night, but it is paged. The `limit` parameter allows at most 25 runs per page (default 20), and the response carries `next_page_token`, which you pass back as `page_token`. A script that reads one page undercounts as the run volume grows, which is a classic cause of counts that stop matching the Jobs UI. `completed_only` and `active_only` are mutually exclusive filters, and `expand_tasks=true` returns task details inside each run. Arrays inside a run are paged too: a single run returns the first 100 elements of `tasks`, `job_clusters`, `job_parameters` and `repair_history`, and `runs/get` returns a `next_page_token` for more. A run that shows Succeeded may have been repaired after an earlier failure; `runs/get` with `include_history=true` (or `--include-history` in the CLI) adds the `repair_history` so on-call can see which repairs happened and when. The CLI mirrors the REST endpoints, so the same pagination rules apply to scripts built on it.

concepts.heading: Task Output, SDK and Authentication
concepts.body: A multi-task job run has one run ID for the job and a separate `run_id` for every task inside `tasks`. `runs/get-output` works on a task run: the value a notebook returns through `dbutils.notebook.exit()` is retrieved by passing the task's `run_id`, taken from `get-run`, and not the job run ID returned by `run-now`. The API returns at most the first 5 MB of output, so larger results should be written to cloud storage. The Databricks SDK for Python implements unified authentication: `WorkspaceClient()` with no arguments discovers credentials from the environment, and the same configuration works for the CLI and other SDKs. For unattended monitors, use a service principal with OAuth machine-to-machine credentials rather than a personal token. Create the client once on the driver and fan out with a thread pool when many objects need polling; creating clients inside Spark executors depends on credentials being available on every worker, which is fragile. The pipelines events endpoint has a similar paging rule: a call with `page_token` may carry only `max_results` besides it, because the token already encodes the filter.

concepts.heading: Where the Pipeline Event Log Lives and Who Can Read It
concepts.body: Every pipeline writes an event log: a record of user actions, update and flow lifecycle, data quality and resource events. By default it is a hidden Delta table named `event_log_<pipeline id>` in the pipeline's default catalog and schema. It is not shown in Catalog Explorer; you read it with the `event_log(<pipeline id>)` table-valued function, and by default only the run-as user of the pipeline may query it. To let an SRE team read it without exposing more, publish the log in the pipeline settings under a name and, optionally, a catalog and schema. Then create a view over the published table and grant `SELECT` on the view, not on the table itself, because the event log location also serves as the schema location for Auto Loader in the pipeline. Views over event logs support streaming queries. Never delete the event log or its parent catalog or schema: the pipeline can fail on later updates. The Jobs-and-pipelines UI, the Pipelines REST API and the log all show the same events.

concepts.heading: What the Event Log Tells You
concepts.body: Pick the event type for the question. `update_progress` describes the lifecycle of an update, so the final state and duration of each update come from the latest such event per `origin.update_id`. `flow_progress` covers the lifecycle of a flow and carries metrics, including `backlog_bytes` and `source_metrics` for sources such as Auto Loader or Kafka, which give an early warning that a running update is falling behind. `planning_information` explains why a materialized view or REPLACE WHERE flow is fully recomputed instead of incrementally refreshed. `operation_progress` events of type `AUTO_LOADER_LISTING` carry `duration_ms` and show when directory listing slows an update before data is processed. `cluster_resources` and `autoscale` events exist only for classic compute, so a serverless pipeline produces none. Data quality sits under `flow_progress`: `dropped_records` counts each dropped row once, while the `expectations` array has `passed_records` and `failed_records` per rule. A row that breaks three rules adds one to each rule, so per-rule failures must not be summed to get the number of bad records.

examPoints: runs/list pages hold at most 25 runs: follow next_page_token with page_token; runs/get with include_history shows repairs.
get-run-output needs the task run_id from get-run, not the job run ID; pipeline event pages after the first take only page_token plus max_results.
Publish the event log, expose a view, grant SELECT on the view. update_progress for update state, flow_progress for backlog and quality, planning_information for MV recompute.

quiz.q: A nightly script calls runs/list with completed_only=true and counts failed runs. As the daily run count grew, the totals stopped matching the Jobs UI although the filter did not change. What is the cause and the fix?
choices: The call returns one page of at most 25 runs, so the script has to follow next_page_token with page_token until none is returned
The completed_only filter hides runs that were repaired, so the script has to call runs/get with include_history for every run it counts
The response truncates the run list at the time window, so the script has to widen start_time_from by one day for every missing run
The endpoint samples runs when a job has many, so the script has to raise the limit to the maximum and call again for the remainder
quiz.explain: runs/list is paginated; each response has at most 25 runs and a next_page_token. Without following it the script sees only the first page. It is not sampling, and repairs are a separate matter.

quiz.q: A materialized view in a pipeline is expected to refresh incrementally, but a refresh after a code change took as long as a full recompute. Which event log information shows how the refresh was planned?
choices: flow_progress events, whose data quality section lists the techniques that the refresh considered and the techniques that it finally rejected
autoscale events, which record the cluster resize requests that forced the planner to choose a complete recompute of the view
update_progress events, whose details state the refresh technique and the reason that an earlier technique was not selected
planning_information events, which list the candidate refresh techniques, the chosen one and any issues that prevented it
quiz.explain: planning_information explains why a materialized view was fully recomputed, including incrementalization issues. flow_progress carries metrics and quality counters, update_progress tracks update state, and autoscale events are only for classic compute resizing.

recap: Page every list call, use task run IDs for output, and read pipeline state from the event log through a published view. Match the event type to the question: update_progress, flow_progress, planning_information, operation_progress.

title: Alerts and Monitoring Runs in the Jobs UI and API

concepts.heading: How an Alert Evaluates
concepts.body: A Databricks SQL alert runs its own query on a schedule against a SQL warehouse and compares one value with a threshold. An evaluation ends as `OK`, `TRIGGERED` or `ERROR`; the older `UNKNOWN` state does not exist in the latest alerts, and each alert owns its query instead of reusing a saved one. The value can come from the first row of a column or from an aggregation across all rows. That choice matters: a query that returns one row per region with the condition on the first value only watches whichever region sorts first, so a drop in another region goes unnoticed. Either make the query return a single summarizing row or select MIN, MAX or SUM in the condition. Advanced settings add Notify on OK for recovery messages, a notification template, and the Empty result state. A freshness check such as `SELECT max(load_time) ... WHERE load_date = current_date()` returns no rows when the load never ran, and by default that does not raise the alert; setting the empty result state to TRIGGERED turns a missing load into a signal.

concepts.heading: Scheduling, Jobs Integration and Git Folders
concepts.body: A workspace limits how many alert runs can be active at once. When all slots are taken at the moment a schedule fires, that run is skipped and the alert does not evaluate; the evaluation history shows a gap with no error. The typical pattern is dozens of alerts sharing one cron time, while a manual Run now works because it runs outside the spike. The fix is to stagger schedules by a few minutes. An alert can also be a task in a job, so downstream tasks can branch on it. That SQL alert task reports Succeeded whenever the alert was evaluated, whether the condition was triggered or not, and Failed only if the evaluation itself errors, so a triggered alert does not fail the run or fire the job's failure notification by itself. It needs a serverless or pro warehouse. Alerts can be tracked in Databricks Git folders, but newly cloned alerts appear in the list only after a user interacts with them, and their schedules are paused until someone resumes each one. After a first release to production, silence usually means paused schedules, not broken queries.

concepts.heading: Monitoring Runs in the Jobs UI
concepts.body: The Runs tab keeps history for 60 days for jobs and pipelines. If auditors need the rendered output of every run for longer, export the notebook run results before they expire and store the files elsewhere, because expired runs and their outputs are not kept. The matrix view shows a history of runs with one bar per run and per task, where the bar height shows duration and the colors show status, so a task that slowly grows over 30 runs is visible without any query. With an expected completion time configured, the matrix warns when a run exceeds it. A `For each` task presents its iterations as a table instead of one cell, and the Only failed iterations toggle reduces 400 iterations to the ones that failed, each opening its own output. Runs sent to `runs/submit`, including those from the Airflow `DatabricksSubmitRunOperator`, are one-time runs without a saved job, so searching by job name finds nothing; filter by Run ID, Run as or Start time, or create a job to get durable, searchable runs.

concepts.heading: Monitoring at Scale with SQL
concepts.body: The UI is for one job; fleets are monitored with SQL. `system.lakeflow.job_run_timeline` and `job_task_run_timeline` give run and task durations and results, so a query can rank tasks by growing duration or count failures per week. The task timeline lists `compute_ids`; joining them to the latest row of `system.compute.clusters` and keeping `cluster_source` values `UI` or `API` finds tasks that run on interactive clusters and should move to job compute. For alerts themselves, `system.alert.alerts` is a slowly changing table of every alert's configuration, and `system.alert.alert_evaluation_history` has one row per evaluation with its evaluated state and error details. A weekly query over evaluations that ended in `ERROR`, or a count of schedules with gaps, finds monitors that are silently broken. These tables are regional, retain data for 395 days for alerts and 365 days for lakeflow, and arrive typically within an hour. Combine them with a Databricks SQL alert on top: monitoring the monitors.

examPoints: Alert conditions read the first row or an aggregation: use MIN/MAX/SUM or a single-row query. Set Empty result state to TRIGGERED when no rows means failure.
Skipped scheduled alert runs come from the active-run limit: stagger schedules. A SQL alert task succeeds whenever evaluation succeeds, triggered or not.
Run history lasts 60 days (export to keep); For each has an Only failed iterations toggle; runs/submit runs have no job name.

quiz.q: An alert query returns one row per region with pct_change, ordered by region name. The condition uses the first value of pct_change below -20. Revenue falls 35% in a region that is not first, and no alert fires. What should the engineer do?
choices: Use an aggregation such as MIN on pct_change in the condition, or return one summarizing row
Set the Empty result state to TRIGGERED, because a region that is not listed first is treated as a missing result by the alert evaluation
Enable Notify on OK, because without a recovery message the alert suppresses every further trigger after its first evaluation
Schedule the alert at a lower frequency, because rows beyond the first are only evaluated when the schedule is stretched out
quiz.explain: The condition looks at the first value only, so other rows are invisible. An aggregation over all rows, or a single-row result, makes every region count. Empty result handling and recovery notifications address different situations.

quiz.q: A job runs a SQL alert task. One morning the alert condition was met, but the task shows Succeeded and the job's failure notification did not fire. How should the engineer interpret this?
choices: The warehouse hit its timeout, because a triggered alert reports success only when the notification destination did not answer
It works as designed: the task succeeds once the alert was evaluated, triggered or not, and fails only if the evaluation errors
The task was skipped by the run-if setting of the job, because alert tasks only report triggered alerts as failures after a full retry cycle
The alert schedule overrode the task, because the job run evaluates the alert on its own cron expression and ignores the result
quiz.explain: The SQL alert task status describes whether the evaluation worked, not whether the condition was met. A triggered alert still means a Succeeded task; downstream tasks or the alert's own subscribers handle the signal.

recap: Alerts need a condition that sees every row, an explicit empty-result state, and staggered schedules. The Jobs UI keeps 60 days of runs; fleets are watched with lakeflow and alert system tables.

title: Managed Tables, Predictive Optimization and Delta Layout Choices

concepts.heading: Managed Tables and Predictive Optimization
concepts.body: Unity Catalog managed tables are the foundation of low-maintenance Delta: Databricks manages the storage location and the table lifecycle. Dropping a managed table deletes its files after a recovery period (7 days by default), while the files of an external table stay in storage until you delete them yourself. Predictive optimization runs `OPTIMIZE`, `VACUUM` and `ANALYZE` on managed tables for you. It can be enabled at account, catalog, schema or table level with inheritance, and the work runs on serverless compute for jobs, so no team cluster is sized for it and the account is billed through a serverless jobs SKU. Two details matter for design. First, `OPTIMIZE` run by predictive optimization does not apply `ZORDER`, and it ignores Z-ordered files, so a nightly Z-order job cannot simply be retired. The path forward is liquid clustering, which it does maintain. Second, its `VACUUM` honors `delta.deletedFileRetentionDuration` (default 7 days): set 30 days before enabling it if time travel of that length is needed.

concepts.heading: Liquid Clustering and Where Its Overhead Goes
concepts.body: Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and `ZORDER`; it cannot be combined with either. You declare `CLUSTER BY (col, ...)` with up to four keys, and data is organized incrementally by `OPTIMIZE`, so changing keys does not rewrite the table. The maintenance burden disappears only if the work runs. Clustering on write happens when a transaction reaches a size threshold, which is lower for managed tables, so a stream appending 5 MB micro-batches leaves new data mostly unclustered and data skipping degrades over weeks. Predictive optimization closes the gap by running incremental clustering in the background. Streaming writes can be clustered on write with `spark.databricks.delta.liquid.eagerClustering.streaming.enabled`, but the size condition still applies. Clustering keys must have statistics: by default only the first 32 columns are covered, so a key in column 70 of a wide table does not skip files until you add it with `delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns` and recompute with `ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS`.

concepts.heading: Choosing a Technique by Access Pattern
concepts.body: Match the technique to the bottleneck. A nightly `MERGE` that touches 0.1% of the rows but scattered over most files is a write problem: without deletion vectors each touched file is rewritten. With deletion vectors changed rows are marked in metadata, reads apply the marks, and files are physically rewritten later, for example by `REORG TABLE ... APPLY (PURGE)` or auto-compaction. Selective dashboard filters are a read problem and call for clustering keys. A table with both patterns uses both, because they address different costs. Deletion vectors upgrade the table protocol, so a client without support fails on reads; in newer runtimes you can drop the feature to restore compatibility. They also block incremental manifest generation: for a Presto-style `GENERATE symlink_format_manifest`, run the purge first with no concurrent writes and then generate. A stable access pattern on external storage can use manual keys, and Z-order on columns without statistics only wastes compute.

concepts.heading: Automatic Clustering and Choosing Keys
concepts.body: `CLUSTER BY AUTO` lets Databricks choose and change keys from the table's query history. It is available only for Unity Catalog managed tables and depends on predictive optimization, which runs the selection asynchronously. It is cost-aware: keys change only when the predicted saving from data skipping outweighs the clustering cost, and it may pick none for tables that are too small or already well ordered. To start from a hint and still adapt, set manual keys first and then enable automatic mode: `ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY (region); ALTER TABLE sales CLUSTER BY AUTO;`. A trap: running `CREATE OR REPLACE TABLE` on an automatic table without `CLUSTER BY AUTO` turns the mode off and drops the chosen columns, so restate the clause. When keys differ strongly in cardinality, hierarchical clustering through `delta.liquid.hierarchicalClusteringColumns` prioritizes a low-cardinality column such as `event_date`; keep high-cardinality columns such as `device_id` as standard keys. Manual hierarchical settings are respected by predictive optimization.

examPoints: Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE (never ZORDER), VACUUM and ANALYZE on managed tables, on serverless jobs compute; set deletedFileRetentionDuration before relying on its VACUUM.
Deletion vectors fix write cost of scattered MERGE; clustering fixes read skipping; they combine. DVs upgrade the protocol and need REORG PURGE before manifest generation.
CLUSTER BY AUTO: managed tables only; CREATE OR REPLACE without it turns it off; clustering keys need statistics (first 32 columns by default).

quiz.q: A team replaced a nightly OPTIMIZE ... ZORDER BY (customer_id) job with predictive optimization. Weeks later, customer_id filters scan more files than before. What explains this and what is the right change?
choices: Predictive optimization runs OPTIMIZE without ZORDER; move the table to liquid clustering on customer_id
Predictive optimization runs VACUUM before OPTIMIZE, so Z-ordered files are removed too early; shorten the retention window to repair the layout
Predictive optimization only starts after 30 days on a table, so the Z-order simply has to wait until the first scheduled run completes
Predictive optimization removes statistics on Z-ordered columns, so the table has to be partitioned by customer_id to regain skipping
quiz.explain: OPTIMIZE run by predictive optimization does not apply ZORDER and ignores Z-ordered files. Liquid clustering is the layout it maintains. There is no 30-day delay, and VACUUM does not reorder files.

quiz.q: Streaming micro-batches of about 5 MB are appended to a liquid-clustered managed table. Data skipping on the clustering keys gets worse over weeks and predictive optimization is turned off. What is the most likely reason and the remedy?
choices: Clustering keys can be changed only with append mode, so the streaming writer silently resets them; use overwrite for every micro-batch
Statistics are collected only for the first 32 columns of the stream schema, so every new key has to be repeated in the stream checkpoint
Small transactions stay below the clustering-on-write threshold; enable predictive optimization so incremental clustering runs
Liquid clustering is rebuilt once per day by VACUUM, so the layout only looks worse until the next scheduled vacuum has finished
quiz.explain: Clustering on write triggers only when a transaction reaches a size threshold, so small batches stay unclustered. Running OPTIMIZE or enabling predictive optimization clusters them incrementally. VACUUM does not cluster data.

recap: Managed tables plus predictive optimization remove most maintenance, but it never runs ZORDER and its VACUUM follows the retention property. Choose deletion vectors for write cost, clustering for read skipping, and CLUSTER BY AUTO for changing patterns on managed tables.

title: Caching for Repeated Reads and Change Data Feed

concepts.heading: The Disk Cache
concepts.body: When a node reads a Parquet file from cloud storage, Databricks copies it to the node's local storage in a fast format, and later reads of the same data run locally. This disk cache serves all Parquet files, including Delta tables, needs no code changes, and is enabled automatically on worker types that support it. The easiest setup is a cache-accelerated worker type with local SSD; network-attached storage only gives no second-read speedup. The cache uses at most half of the local SSD space by default. It detects created, deleted, modified and overwritten files and evicts stale entries by itself, so after a `MERGE` or `OPTIMIZE` nobody has to invalidate anything, and jobs that try are unnecessary. On SQL warehouses and recent runtimes `CACHE SELECT` is ignored because an enhanced disk caching algorithm is used instead, so a manual warm-up step does nothing. To measure cold reads for a benchmark, set `spark.databricks.io.cache.enabled` to `false`: queries then neither read from nor add to the cache, and nothing needs to be deleted.

concepts.heading: Disk Cache versus Spark Cache
concepts.body: The two caches solve different problems. The disk cache stores copies of source files on local disk; it makes repeated scans of the same files cheap but stores no transformation results. The Apache Spark cache, created with `df.cache()` or `persist`, stores a DataFrame's computed partitions in memory and on disk. If a heavy join and aggregation result feeds five actions, persisting that DataFrame avoids repeating the join, which the disk cache cannot do. The Spark cache has a weakness on elastic clusters: when a worker is decommissioned by autoscaling, the cached blocks on it are lost and Spark rereads or recomputes the missing partitions, so the second report can be slower than the first although the data is unchanged. Release it with `unpersist` when finished. The Databricks recommendation for repeated reads of Parquet and Delta data is the automatic disk cache; reserve the Spark cache for expensive intermediate results reused several times in one session. On serverless compute `df.cache()` behaves differently from the classic Spark cache.

concepts.heading: Change Data Feed for Incremental Downstream Processing
concepts.body: Change data feed exposes row-level changes between table versions: each change row carries the data plus `_change_type` (`insert`, `update_preimage`, `update_postimage`, `delete`), `_commit_version` and a timestamp. Two forms exist, both read with `table_changes()` or the `readChangeFeed` option. Legacy CDF is switched on with `delta.enableChangeDataFeed` and writes change data at write time, which costs write overhead and storage on heavy `MERGE` and `UPDATE` jobs. Automatic CDF computes changes at read time from row tracking (Delta) or row lineage (Iceberg v3), so it needs no per-table setting and adds no write cost; it needs managed or external Delta tables with row tracking on a recent runtime. You cannot use both: to migrate, unset the legacy property and keep the same read code. CDF is transient: the feed is removed with old versions and `VACUUM`, so it is not an audit trail. For a permanent history, run a `readChangeFeed` stream, for example with an `availableNow` trigger and its own checkpoint, that appends the changes to a separate history table.

concepts.heading: Reading the Feed Correctly
concepts.body: Several rows can describe one key. An update yields a `update_preimage` and a `update_postimage` row, and a key changed in several commits appears repeatedly in a version range. Feeding that raw range into a `MERGE` fails with a multiple-match error. Drop the preimage rows, keep the highest `_commit_version` per key, and apply deletes where `_change_type = 'delete'`. In Structured Streaming, Databricks tracks the version for you through the checkpoint; if the checkpoint is lost, start a new stream with a new checkpoint and `startingVersion` set to one more than the last version the target already reflects, not at zero. A batch hourly job that stores its own last version can fail on quiet hours because the start version is beyond the last commit; setting `spark.databricks.delta.changeDataFeed.timestampOutOfRange.enabled` makes it return an empty result. On tables with column mapping, a query cannot span a non-additive schema change such as a rename or drop: split the range into parts before and after it.

examPoints: Disk cache: automatic, SSD workers, evicts stale files by itself, ignores CACHE SELECT on warehouses. Spark cache stores results but is lost when autoscaling removes workers.
Automatic CDF (row tracking, no write overhead) replaces legacy delta.enableChangeDataFeed; both cannot be active together, and the read APIs stay the same.
CDF is transient: keep history in your own table. Dedupe preimage/postimage rows by key and latest _commit_version; restart a stream at last applied version + 1.

quiz.q: A notebook computes a heavy join and aggregation and then uses the resulting DataFrame in five actions. The cluster has SSD workers with the disk cache on, but the join still runs five times. What reduces the repeated work?
choices: Persist the joined DataFrame with the Spark cache, because the disk cache holds source file copies, not results
Run CACHE SELECT on the source tables first, because that command stores the join output in the disk cache on every single worker
Enable the disk cache at the notebook level, because the cluster setting does not apply to DataFrames that were created from joins
Switch the workers to network-attached storage, because local SSD copies of the files force every action to recompute the join
quiz.explain: The disk cache stores source file copies; it does not keep the result of a join. df.cache() or persist keeps the computed partitions for later actions. CACHE SELECT does not store transformation output.

quiz.q: A downstream job reads table_changes('customers', 41, 45) and merges every row into a dimension table. Several customers appear more than once with update_preimage and update_postimage rows, and the MERGE fails with a multiple-match error. What is the fix?
choices: Run the MERGE with delete semantics only, because preimage rows are the correct images of every customer in the range
Read each version on its own, because a range query is not supported once more than one commit touches the same customer
Disable row tracking on the table, because the duplicate rows come from automatic change data feed and not from the table itself
Drop update_preimage rows, keep the highest _commit_version row per customer_id, and apply deletes from _change_type = 'delete'
quiz.explain: A range can contain several changes per key plus preimage images. Keeping the newest postimage per key and applying deletes gives one source row per target row. Range reads are supported and the duplicates are normal in the feed.

recap: Rely on the automatic disk cache for repeated file reads and use persist only for reused results, remembering that autoscaling drops Spark cache blocks. Use change data feed for incremental processing, keep your own history, and deduplicate change rows per key.

title: Query Profile Bottlenecks and Liquid Clustering versus Partitioning

concepts.heading: Reading the Query Profile and Its Insights
concepts.body: The query profile shows the plan as a graph with per-operator metrics, and Databricks attaches performance insights ranked by their estimated effect on total task duration. Start from the insight, then confirm it in the operators. A query answered from the query cache has no profile; to capture one, make a trivial change such as changing or removing the `LIMIT`. `EXPLODING_JOIN` flags a join that outputs far more rows than it reads, for example 3 million orders against 50,000 customers producing 900 million rows: check whether the join key is unique on the dimension side, then deduplicate it or tighten the join condition. `SELECTIVE_JOIN` suggests filtering before the join, `WIDE_PROJECTION` suggests selecting only needed columns, and `REDUNDANT_JOIN` and `REDUNDANT_AGGREGATION` point to work that did not change the result. `COVERAGE_FILTER_KEYS_CLUSTERING` and its partitioning twin mean filters do not use the table's layout keys, so adding filters on those keys reduces bytes read. Insights labelled Accelerated, such as `HISTORY_BASED_JOIN_STRATEGY`, describe optimizations Databricks already applied and need no action.

concepts.heading: Data Layout Insights
concepts.body: `COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA` says file-skipping statistics are missing or incomplete for the scan's filters, with a status of Full, Partial, Unavailable or Unused (the filter converts the data type). The remedy is to make the filtered column a statistics column with `delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns` and recompute with `ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS` so existing files get statistics. By default external tables collect statistics on the first 32 columns, so a filter on column 80 of a wide table scans nearly everything. `DATA_FILE_SIZE` reports many small files: enable predictive optimization or run `OPTIMIZE`, and for a partitioned table consider liquid clustering, because predictive optimization cannot compact small files across partitions. `DATA_SKEW` means uneven distribution, as when 70% of rows have a NULL key; the remedy is key salting or pre-aggregation in two stages, group by the key and a random salt first and then combine. `MANUAL_DATA_LAYOUT` recommends managed tables, predictive optimization and automatic clustering, and `CONCURRENT_WRITE` points to conflicts that need scheduling or a layout with row-level concurrency.

concepts.heading: Compute Insights and Plan Differences
concepts.body: `DATA_SPILL` means data did not fit in memory. When the warehouse size is fixed by policy, reduce what the operators carry: select only needed columns before the join and sort, so a 4 KB `raw_payload` string is not held in memory for every row. `EXCESSIVE_QUEUE_TIME` appears when a query's wall-clock time is mostly waiting for warehouse capacity, for example dozens of dashboards refreshing at 09:00; the recommendation is a higher maximum number of clusters, which adds capacity when queries queue, while execution time itself is fine. `IO_THROTTLING` points to cloud storage request limits and is a matter for administrators. Plans can legitimately differ between `EXPLAIN` and the profile. `SQL EXPLAIN` does not run the query, so adaptive query execution cannot re-optimize it and shows only the initial plan, for instance a sort merge join; the executed query can switch to a broadcast join when runtime statistics show a small side. Trust the profile of the real run, and do not add a hint that forces broadcast when the optimizer already chose it from history, because the hint stays forced even if the table grows.

concepts.heading: Liquid Clustering versus Partitioning and ZORDER
concepts.body: Choose liquid clustering for new tables, especially with high-cardinality filters, skew, fast growth, concurrent writers or changing patterns; it is incompatible with partitioning and `ZORDER`. Telemetry filtered by `device_id` (millions of values) and a recent `event_date` range suits `CLUSTER BY (event_date, device_id)` with predictive optimization, not a partition on `device_id`. Keys accept struct fields in dot notation such as `device.model`. A table that was fast through natural ingestion order but degrades under scattered `UPDATE` and `MERGE` gains from clustering on a matching date column. Clustering also allows row-level concurrency, so concurrent `MERGE` jobs touching different rows of the same partition conflict far less. To convert a partitioned Delta table, use `ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY`, keep the new columns close to the old partition columns to avoid a large first `OPTIMIZE`, and run `OPTIMIZE`. Managed Iceberg tables already use partition definitions as clustering keys, so the command errors for them. For a pipeline streaming table, change `PARTITIONED BY` to `CLUSTER BY` in the source. Clustered Delta tables need writer version 7 and reader version 3, so older readers may need the old layout.

examPoints: Read the insight first: EXPLODING_JOIN (check key uniqueness), COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA (statistics columns + ANALYZE), DATA_SKEW (salt or pre-aggregate), EXCESSIVE_QUEUE_TIME (max clusters).
A cached query has no profile (change LIMIT). SQL EXPLAIN shows the initial plan only; AQE changes it at run time, so trust the profile.

Liquid clustering replaces partitioning and ZORDER; convert with REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY; managed Iceberg errors; pipeline tables change their definition; old readers keep the old layout.

quiz.q: A selective query on a wide external Delta table filters on tenant_id and scans nearly every file. Its profile shows a COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA insight. Which action addresses the cause?
choices: Raise the maximum number of clusters of the warehouse, because missing file statistics are caused by queries that wait in the queue
Add tenant_id to delta.dataSkippingStatsColumns and run ANALYZE TABLE ... COMPUTE DELTA STATISTICS so existing files get statistics
Partition the table by tenant_id, because partition pruning is the only technique that skips files for columns without any statistics
Rewrite the filter with a salting expression, because the insight reports that the filtered column is distributed unevenly across tasks
quiz.explain: COVERAGE_STATS_DELTA means file-skipping statistics are missing or incomplete for the filtered column. Declaring it a statistics column and recomputing statistics lets existing files be skipped. Queue time and skew are different insights.

quiz.q: A 200 GB Delta table is partitioned by event_hour with about 9,000 partitions of roughly 20 MB, and scans read thousands of small files. Predictive optimization cannot compact them. The conversion should cause minimal downtime. What should the engineer do?
choices: Run ALTER TABLE ... REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY (event_hour), then OPTIMIZE
Add ZORDER BY (event_hour) to a nightly OPTIMIZE, because Z-ordering merges the small files of different partitions into one larger file
Partition the table by event_minute instead, because smaller partitions reduce the number of files that a scan has to open
Run VACUUM with a retention of zero hours, because deleting old versions compacts the small files of every partition
quiz.explain: Predictive optimization cannot compact small files across partitions, so liquid clustering is the route. The conversion minimizes reader and writer downtime, and keeping the keys near the old partition columns avoids a large first reclustering.

recap: Start from the performance insight, confirm it in the profile, and fix its cause: key uniqueness, statistics, skew, spill, queue time. Prefer liquid clustering over partitioning and ZORDER, and convert partitioned tables with REPLACE PARTITIONED BY WITH CLUSTER BY.
